text.tspan: Everyday English - C2 - 2026/03/27 - Essay - 01
People share a meal and conversation.
Pexels · 9220890
Around the table
To share a meal is to negotiate a familiar but frequently obscured relationship between intentional design and the contingencies of shared experience. The
question is not whether arrangements are desirable, but what authority they should acquire. A credible position supports preparation while withholding the
assumption that procedural coherence is equivalent to human value.
There is a substantive case for structure: a simple plan leaves time for conversation. Here, we prepare the vegetables before our guests arrive. The
arrangement earns its legitimacy through the specific difficulty it alleviates, not through its conformity to an abstract ideal of order. Its success is
consequently conditional. Once the intervention demands more attention than the obstacle it removes, the original justification begins to unravel.
An assessment confined to that practical benefit would nevertheless be incomplete, since sharing the work helps everyone feel included. In concrete
terms, each guest brings one dish and helps clear the table. This introduces a problem of perspective: whose convenience supplies the standard against
which improvement is measured? An apparently neutral procedure may privilege the preferences of its designer. Attentiveness to others makes that
asymmetry visible and creates grounds for revision.
What emerges is a qualified defence of planning, rather than a celebration of either control or spontaneity. Arrangements can sustain an experience
without exhausting its meaning. Their authority should remain answerable to the people and circumstances they affect; otherwise, a means of making life
more habitable risks becoming the criterion to which life must conform.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion. Each body paragraph
needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.
Write about an attempt to share a meal that did not go as planned. Explain two lessons, each supported by a specific incident. Use four short paragraphs:
introduction, two developed points, and conclusion. (Model: One possible outline: introduce the situation; discuss a simple plan leaves time for
conversation with an example; discuss sharing the work helps everyone feel included with a different example; conclude by connecting the two points.)
